'''Eric Emil Schadt''' (born January 31, 1965) is an American mathematician and [[computational biology|computational biologist]]. He is founder and former [[chief executive officer]] of [[Sema4]], a patient-centered health intelligence company, and dean for precision medicine and Mount Sinai Professor in Predictive Health and Computational Biology at the [[Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai]]. He was previously founding director of the [[Icahn Institute for Genomics and Multiscale Biology]] and chair of the Department of Genetics and Genomics Sciences at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai.

Schadt's work combines supercomputing and advanced computational modeling with diverse biological data to understand the relationship between genes, gene products, other molecular features such as cells, organs, organisms, and communities and their impact on complex human traits such as disease.<ref name="nytimes1">{{cite news|author=David Ewing Duncan |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/08/25/science/25prof.html?pagewanted=all |title=Enlisting Computers to Unravel the True Complexity of Disease |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=2009-08-24 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> He is known for calling for a shift in molecular biology toward a [[Systems biology|network-oriented view of living systems]] to complement the [[Reductionism|reductionist]], single-gene approaches that currently dominate biology to more accurately model the complexity of biological systems.<ref name="esquire1">{{cite web|last=Junod |first=Tom |url=https://www.esquire.com/features/eric-schadt-0411 |title=Eric Schadt Profile - Interview with Eric Schadt Pacific Biosciences |website=Esquire.com |date=2011-03-22 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref><ref name="genengnews1">{{cite web |url=http://genengnews.com/gen-articles/the-b-schadt-b-equation/4694/ |title=The Schadt Equation &#124; GEN |website=Genengnews.com |date=2013-01-15 |access-date=2017-06-17 |archive-date=2018-02-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180210004602/https://genengnews.com/gen-articles/the-b-schadt-b-equation/4694/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Schadt has also worked to engage the public, encouraging people to participate in scientific research and helping them understand privacy concerns around DNA-based information.<ref name="nature1">{{cite journal|author=Schadt EE|date=2012|title=The changing privacy landscape in the era of big data|journal=Molecular Systems Biology|volume=8|page=612|doi=10.1038/msb.2012.47|pmid=22968446|pmc=3472686}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scientificamerican.com/article/genetic-heroes-may-be-key-to-treating-debilitating-diseases/ |title="Genetic Heroes" May Be Key to Treating Debilitating Diseases |publisher=Scientific American |date=2014-05-30 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref>

== Research and training ==
In 1983, Schadt left high school early to enlist in the [[United States Air Force]] and joined a Special Operations/Rescue unit. After sustaining a serious shoulder injury that required reconstructive surgery, Schadt attended [[California Polytechnic State University]] on a military scholarship to study computer science and mathematics, and received his bachelor's degree in applied mathematics in 1991.<ref name="nytimes1"/> He went on to earn a master's degree in pure mathematics at the [[University of California, Davis]] in 1993. After that, he pursued a PhD in biomathematics at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], which required PhD candidacy in both molecular biology and biomathematics, completing his doctorate under the supervision of Ken Lange in 2000.<ref name="genengnews1"/> During his PhD work, Schadt worked as a senior software engineer at the UCLA Office of Academic Computing and later as director of computing in the UCLA mathematical sciences department{{Citation needed|date = December 2015}}.

== Scientific career ==

=== Early career ===
While completing his PhD, Schadt joined Roche Bioscience in 1998 as a senior research scientist and began his work on DNA microarrays, designing novel algorithms to process and interpret these data. He published some of the first independently developed algorithms to process gene chip data<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Schadt, E. E.|author2=Li, C.|author3=Su, C.|author4=Wong, W. H.|title= Analyzing high-density oligonucleotide gene expression array data. |journal=Journal of Cellular Biochemistry |volume=80|issue=2|pages=192–202 |date=2000|url=https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/cli/pdf/Schadt_00.pdf |doi=10.1002/1097-4644(20010201)80:2<192::aid-jcb50>3.3.co;2-n|pmid=11074587}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Schadt, E. E.|author2=Li, C.|author3=Su, C.|author4=Wong, W. H.|title=Feature extraction and normalization algorithms for high-density oligonucleotide gene expression array data|journal=Journal of Cellular Biochemistry|volume=Supplement Suppl 37|pages=120–125|date=2001|url=http://linkage.rockefeller.edu/microarray/schadt02.pdf|doi=10.1002/jcb.10073|pmid=11842437|s2cid=6810381}}</ref> work that he later applied to produce an early whole genome functional annotation of the human genome.<ref name="autogenerated2001">{{cite journal|author=Shoemaker, D. D.|display-authors=etal|title=Experimental annotation of the human genome using microarray technology|journal=Nature |volume=409|issue=6822|pages=922–927|doi=10.1038/35057141 |pmid=11237012|date=2001|url=http://www.ccmm.ma/documents/cours%20de%20genome/References/Experimental%20annotation%20of%20the%20human%20genome%20using%20microarray%20technology.pdf|bibcode=2001Natur.409..922S|s2cid=2509337|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 1999, after becoming acquainted with [[Stephen Friend]], he was hired as chief scientist at Rosetta Inpharmatics, a startup biotech company focused on the generation and analysis of high-dimensional [[functional genomics]] data.<ref name="nytimes1"/> Merck acquired Rosetta in 2001, which allowed Schadt to combine large-scale molecular profiling with Merck's disease-focused databases to demonstrate the existence of molecular networks working together to give rise to [[complex system]] behavior.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Schadt, E. E.|display-authors=etal|title= Genetics of gene expression surveyed in maize, mouse and man|journal=Nature|volume=422|issue=6929|pages=297–302|doi=10.1038/nature01434|pmid=12646919|date=2003|bibcode=2003Natur.422..297S|s2cid=2559717}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Schadt, E. E.|author2=Monks, S. A.|author3=Friend, S. H.|title=A new paradigm for drug discovery: integrating clinical, genetic, genomic and molecular phenotype data to identify drug targets|journal=Biochemical Society Transactions|volume=31|issue=2|pages=437–443|date=2003|url=http://test.biochemsoctrans.org/bst/031/0437/bst0310437.htm|doi=10.1042/bst0310437|pmid=12653656|access-date=2013-01-30|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130414123524/http://test.biochemsoctrans.org/bst/031/0437/bst0310437.htm|archive-date=2013-04-14|url-status=dead|url-access=subscription}}</ref> During this period Schadt developed his theory that single-gene approaches to understanding and treating common human diseases must give way to a network-based approach and that many of the failures in pharmaceutical therapies were caused by an incomplete understanding of biology underlying the therapeutic targets.<ref name="esquire1"/>

Demonstrating the ability to infer causal relationships among features in high dimensional data using DNA variation information, Schadt and his colleagues at [[Merck & Co.|Merck]] began reconstructing predictive networks that were shown to be causally associated with disease,<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Schadt, E. E.|author2=Sachs, A.|author3=Friend, S.|title= Embracing complexity, inching closer to reality|journal= Science's STKE|date=2005|page=40|doi=10.1126/stke.2952005pe40 |pmid=16077086|url=http://pubget.com/paper/16077086/Embracing_complexity__inching_closer_to_reality|volume=2005|issue=295|s2cid=23744520|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
<ref>{{cite journal|author=Chen, Y.|display-authors=etal|title=Variations in DNA elucidate molecular networks that cause disease|journal=Nature |volume=452|issue=7186|pages=429–435|doi=10.1038/nature06757 |pmid=18344982|date=2008|pmc=2841398|bibcode=2008Natur.452..429C}}</ref>
<ref>{{cite journal|author=Emilsson, V.|display-authors=etal|title=Genetics of gene expression and its effect on disease|journal=Nature|volume=452|issue=7186|pages=423–428|doi=10.1038/nature06758|pmid=18344981|date=2008|bibcode=2008Natur.452..423E|s2cid=1219108}}</ref>
<ref>{{cite journal|author=Schadt, E. E.|title=Molecular networks as sensors and drivers of common human diseases|journal=Nature|volume=461|issue=7261|pages=218–223|doi=10.1038/nature08454 |pmid=19741703|date=2009|bibcode=2009Natur.461..218S|s2cid=4323333}}</ref>
<ref>{{cite journal|author=Yang, X.|display-authors=etal|title= Validation of candidate causal genes for obesity that affect shared metabolic pathways and networks|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=41|issue=4|pages=415–423|doi=10.1038/ng.325 |pmid=19270708|date=2009|pmc=2837947}}</ref> leading to the idea of targeting networks, not single genes, to effectively treat common disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, obesity, and most forms of cancer.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Schadt, E. E.|author2=Friend, S. H.|author3=Shaywitz, D. A. |title=A network view of disease and compound screening|journal=Nature Reviews Drug Discovery|volume=8|issue=4|pages=286–295|doi=10.1038/nrd2826|pmid=19337271|date=2009|s2cid=21562023}}</ref> A Merck spokesman said that the papers Schadt began publishing based on this genetic network data “changed the way people looked at disease.” Schadt used the information about these networks to determine which genes Merck should pursue as targets; by the time he left the company, Schadt estimated that his group was responsible for half the drugs in the company's development pipeline.<ref name="nytimes1"/>

In 2009, along with Stephen Friend, Schadt founded [[Sage Bionetworks]],<ref name="genengnews1"/> a nonprofit organization with the goal of encouraging collaboration between academic and commercial scientists in performing network-based studies of disease and making the data publicly available. When Merck closed down the Rosetta business unit, it donated the data, research, and computer equipment from that unit to Sage Bionetworks.<ref name="nytimes1"/> Schadt remains involved as a board member.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://sagebase.org/info/directors.php |title=Sage Bionetworks Seattle &#124; Directors |access-date=2013-01-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120127081638/http://sagebase.org/info/directors.php |archive-date=2012-01-27 }}</ref>

Also in 2009, Schadt joined [[DNA sequencing]] company [[Pacific Biosciences]] as the chief scientific officer. During his time there, Schadt demonstrated the application of [[SMRT sequencing]] technology for various applications,<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Schadt, E. E.|author2=Turner, S.|author3=Kasarskis, A.|title=A window into third-generation sequencing|journal=Human Molecular Genetics |volume=19|issue=R2|doi=10.1093/hmg/ddq416 |pmid=20858600|date=2010|pages=R227–R240|doi-access=free}}</ref> including to sequence bacterial genomes of public health concern to provide real-time information about these pathogenic strains during an active outbreak. He led research projects to resolve the origins of the [[2010–2013 Haiti cholera outbreak|Haitian cholera outbreak]] strain from 2010<ref>{{cite journal|author=Chin, C. S.|display-authors=etal|title=The origin of the Haitian cholera outbreak strain|journal=The New England Journal of Medicine |volume=364|issue=1|pages=33–42|doi=10.1056/NEJMoa1012928 |pmid=21142692|date=2011|pmc=3030187}}</ref> and to characterize the highly virulent [[2011 Germany E. coli O104:H4 outbreak|German E. coli outbreak]] strain in the summer of 2011.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Rasko, D. A.|display-authors=etal|title=Origins of the E. coli strain causing an outbreak of hemolytic-uremic syndrome in Germany. |journal=The New England Journal of Medicine|volume=365|issue=8|pages=709–717|doi=10.1056/NEJMoa1106920 |pmid=21793740|date=2011|pmc=3168948}}</ref> He also demonstrated the ability to infer [[Epigenetics|epigenetic]] changes from the sequencing data, uncovering novel regulatory mechanisms that may impact pathogenicity and virulence of bacteria of concern in public health.<ref name="nature2">{{cite journal|author=Fang, G.|display-authors=etal|title=Genome-wide mapping of methylated adenine residues in pathogenic Escherichia coli using single-molecule real-time sequencing|journal= Nature Biotechnology|volume=30|issue=12|pages=1232–1239|doi=10.1038/nbt.2432 |pmid=23138224|pmc=3879109|date=2012}}</ref>
<ref>{{cite journal|author=Schadt, E. E.|display-authors=etal|title=Modeling kinetic rate variation in third generation DNA sequencing data to detect putative modifications to DNA bases. |volume=23|issue=1|pages=129–141|doi=10.1101/gr.136739.111|pmid=23093720|date=2013|journal=Genome Research|pmc=3530673}}</ref>

=== Mount Sinai ===
In 2011, Schadt joined the Mount Sinai School of Medicine in New York, where he founded the new Icahn Institute for Genomics and Multiscale Biology and became chair of the Department of Genetics and Genomics Sciences.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mssm.edu/about-us/news-and-events/eric-schadt-phd-named-director-of-institute-for-genomics-and-multiscale-biology-at-the-mount-sinai-medical-center |title=Eric Schadt, PhD, Named Director of Institute for Genomics and Multiscale Biology at The Mount Sinai Medical Center - Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai |website=Mssm.edu |date= |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.bio-itworld.com/news/05/16/2011/PacBio-CSO-Eric-Schadt-Lead-Multiscale-institute-Mt-Sinai.html |title=PacBio CSO Eric Schadt to Lead 'Multiscale Institute' at Mount Sinai - Bio-IT World |access-date=2013-01-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110730165839/http://www.bio-itworld.com/news/05/16/2011/PacBio-CSO-Eric-Schadt-Lead-Multiscale-institute-Mt-Sinai.html |archive-date=2011-07-30 }}</ref><ref name="nytimes2">{{cite web |url=http://prescriptions.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/05/16/schadt-joins-mount-sinai-medical-school/ |title=Eric Schadt of Pacific Biosciences Joins Mount Sinai - NYTimes.com |access-date=2013-01-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130224130451/http://prescriptions.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/05/16/schadt-joins-mount-sinai-medical-school/ |archive-date=2013-02-24 }}</ref> The new institute was launched with $100 million for the first five years and is co-directed by [[Andrew Kasarskis]].<ref name="nytimes2"/> Schadt has said that his interest in joining Mt. Sinai was to bring predictive modeling of biology to patients. In his time at the institute, he has opened the first CLIA-certified next-generation sequencing lab in New York City<ref>{{cite journal|title=Eric Schadt |doi=10.1038/nbt.2331|pmid=22871721 |volume=30|issue=8 |year=2012|journal=Nature Biotechnology|pages=769–770|last1=Schadt |first1=E. |doi-access=free}}</ref> and established the first class at the school in which students sequence their own genomes.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.genomeweb.com/sequencing/qa-mount-sinais-andrew-kasarskis-teaching-students-how-analyze-their-own-genomes |title=Q&A: Mount Sinai's Andrew Kasarskis on Teaching Students how to Analyze their Own Genomes |website=GenomeWeb.com |date=2012-10-24 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://issuu.com/johndavey/docs/genomics_annual_report_fnl?e=4406893/7703943 |title=Genomics annual report fnl by Mount Sinai Health System |website=Issuu.com |date=2014-05-02 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> Schadt also serves on the executive committee of the [[New York Genome Center]].

In 2013, Schadt and his team were awarded a grant from the [[National Institutes of Health]] to study biological networks in [[Alzheimer's disease]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nih.gov/news/health/sep2013/nia-18.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130919013240/http://www.nih.gov/news/health/sep2013/nia-18.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 19, 2013 |title=NIH funding boosts new Alzheimer's research on prevention, novel drug targets &#124; National Institutes of Health (NIH) |website=Nih.gov |date=2013-09-18 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> They also published a paper in Cell reporting that a network of genes linked to inflammatory response plays a role in late-onset Alzheimer's disease.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cell.com/abstract/S0092-8674(13)00387-5 |title=Cell - Integrated Systems Approach Identifies Genetic Nodes and Networks in Late-Onset Alzheimer's Disease |website=www.cell.com |access-date=27 January 2022 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130713030433/http://www.cell.com/abstract/S0092-8674(13)00387-5 |archive-date=13 July 2013 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://health.usnews.com/health-news/news/articles/2013/04/25/gene-studies-could-point-to-new-alzheimers-treatments |title=Gene Studies Could Point to New Alzheimer's Treatments - US News |access-date=2014-08-18 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819083406/http://health.usnews.com/health-news/news/articles/2013/04/25/gene-studies-could-point-to-new-alzheimers-treatments |archive-date=2014-08-19 }}</ref> Also that year, Schadt joined the [[Cure Alzheimer's Fund]]'s Research Consortium along with [[Richard L. Huganir]].

Schadt's team was cited as the reason the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai was named #5 of the top 10 most innovative organizations in big data by Fast Company in a 2014 ranking.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fastcompany.com/most-innovative-companies/2014/industry/big-data |title=The Most Innovative Companies of 2014 by Sector |work=Fast Company |date= 10 February 2014|access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> According to the article, "The New York City hospital is bringing on top Silicon Valley talent to build a facility that will map patients’ genomes to predict diseases, reduce the number of average hospital visits, and streamline electronic medical records."

In May 2014, Schadt and his team announced [[the Resilience Project]] in collaboration with Sage Bionetworks.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Friend |first=Stephen H. |url=https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.1255648 |title=Clues from the resilient &#124; Science |journal=Science |date=2014-05-30 |volume=344 |issue=6187 |pages=970–972 |doi=10.1126/science.1255648 |pmid=24876479 |s2cid=26492504 |access-date=2017-06-17|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The project  intended to perform genotyping on as many as 1 million people to find protective biological mechanisms that prevent disease-causing genetic mutations from becoming active. Participants were to be healthy people age 30 and older, and the project initially targeted variations linked to 127 Mendelian diseases.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2014/05/searching-for-the-genes-that-prevent-disease/371256/ |title=The Search for Genes That Prevent Disease |publisher=[[The Atlantic]] |date=2014-05-29 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://resilienceproject.me/ |title=The Resilience Project &#124; Join the Search. Be a Hero |website=Resilienceproject.me |date=2016-04-11 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> Based on an analysis of publicly available data, scientists in the Resilience Project estimated that one person in 15,000 has a protective mechanism preventing activity of disease-causing genetic variants.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.fastcoexist.com/3027995/searching-for-the-hidden-health-heroes-whose-dna-prevents-disease |title=Searching For The Hidden Health Heroes Whose DNA Prevents Disease |website=Fastcoexist.com |date=2014-05-29 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> The project led to a paper published in 2016 in [[Nature Biotechnology]], reporting the analysis of nearly 600,000 genomes and the identification of individuals resilient to severe Mendelian childhood diseases.

=== Sema4 ===
Schadt founded Sema4, "a patient-centered health intelligence company dedicated to advancing healthcare through data-driven insights,"<ref name="Our Story">{{Cite web|title=Our Story |url=https://sema4.com/our-story/|website=Sema4.com |access-date=2021-04-12}}</ref> in June 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Introducing Sema4: A Spinout Company of the Mount Sinai Health System {{!}} Mount Sinai - New York|url=https://www.mountsinai.org/about/newsroom/2017/introducing-sema4-a-spinout-company-of-the-mount-sinai-health-system|access-date=2021-03-16|website=Mount Sinai Health System|language=en-US}}</ref> The company uses Centrellis™, their health analytics platform, to build predictive models of human health and generate [[personalized medicine]] insights.<ref name="Our Story"/> Sema4, which was named one of the 150 most promising private digital health companies in the world by CB Insights in its 2020 Digital Health 150 ranking,<ref>{{Cite web|title= Sema4 Named to the 2020 CB Insights Digital Health 150, a List of the Most Innovative Digital Health Startups|url=https://money.yahoo.com/sema4-named-2020-cb-insights-140000863.html |access-date=2021-04-20}}</ref> operates two state-of-the art clinical laboratories in Connecticut, including a 70,000-square-foot facility opened in December 2020<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://westfaironline.com/130757/sema4-opens-70000-square-foot-clinical-lab-in-stamford/|title=Sema4 opens 70,000-square-foot clinical lab in Stamford |date=3 December 2020 |access-date=2021-04-12}}</ref> The company announced in February 2021 that it would be going public through a merger with CM Life Sciences, a [[Special-purpose acquisition company|special purpose acquisition company]] (SPAC).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Sema4 to Go Public Through Merger With Special Purpose Acquisition Company|url=https://www.genomeweb.com/business-news/sema4-go-public-through-merger-special-purpose-acquisition-company|access-date=2021-03-16|website=GenomeWeb|date=10 February 2021 |language=en-us}}</ref>

== Media appearances and awards ==
Schadt has appeared on CNN, CNBC, BBC, Bloomberg Radio, and Bloomberg TV.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/videos/2015-03-11/how-the-iphone-is-helping-doctors-battle-diseases |title=How the iPhone is Helping Doctors Battle Diseases |website=Bloomberg.com|date=11 March 2015 }}</ref> He and his scientific projects have been profiled in the New York Times, Esquire magazine,<ref name="esquire1"/> [[Bloomberg Businessweek|Bloomberg BusinessWeek]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.businessweek.com/articles/2014-03-06/icahn-institutes-eric-schadt-on-data-analysis-in-medicine |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140815134800/http://www.businessweek.com/articles/2014-03-06/icahn-institutes-eric-schadt-on-data-analysis-in-medicine |url-status=dead |archive-date=August 15, 2014 |title=Icahn Institute's Eric Schadt on Data Analysis in Medicine - Bloomberg |website=Businessweek.com |date=2014-03-06 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> among others,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.macleans.ca/society/health/the-little-girl-who-may-hold-the-secret-to-aging/ |title=The little girl who may hold the secret to aging |website=Macleans.ca |date=2014-07-20 |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> and several scientific trade publications. [[HuffPost|The Huffington Post]] published a commentary by Schadt, calling on scientists to incorporate information about RNA, proteins, metabolites and more into their genetic or clinical research, while asking the public to participate in research projects to help speed scientific discovery.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/eric-e-schadt/its-not-just-the-genes_b_4156281.html |title=It's Not Just the Genes &#124; HuffPost |website=Huffingtonpost.com |date= 24 October 2013|access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> Schadt has also spoken at numerous events including [[TEDMED]], the health/medicine edition of the world-famous TED conference.

He has received many awards, including the Thomson Reuters World's Most Influential Scientific Minds Award<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sciencewatch.com/sites/sw/files/sw-article/media/worlds-most-influential-scientific-minds-2014.pdf |title=The World's Most Influential Scientific Minds |date=2014 |website=Sciencewatch.com |access-date=2017-06-17}}</ref> and the Merck Presidential Fellowship Award. He was executive producer and creative director of a documentary film called “The New Biology” that won a Cine Master Series Award in 2012.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.johnrubin.com/images/jd_cv.pdf |title=Archived copy |access-date=2013-01-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130120151951/http://www.johnrubin.com/images/jd_cv.pdf |archive-date=2013-01-20 }}</ref> In 2020, Schadt was named the BioCT Entrepreneur of the Year.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bioct.org/2020/12/09/eric-schadt-founder-ceo-of-sema4-named-2020-bioct-entrepreneur-of-the-year/ |title=Eric Schadt, Founder & CEO of Sema4, Named 2020 BioCT Entrepreneur of the Year |work=BioCT |date=9 December 2020 |access-date=2021-04-12}}</ref>

== Selected publications ==
Schadt has published more than 370 [[Peer review|peer-reviewed]] papers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Schadt%2C+ee |title=schadt, ee - search results | website=PubMed |access-date=2021-04-20}}</ref> He is a highly cited author, with an [[h-index]] of 129 and more than 145,500 citations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=s18-KHUAAAAJ |title=Eric Schadt - Google Scholar |access-date=2021-04-20}}</ref> Some notable publications include:

* A Nature Genetics paper<ref>{{cite journal|author=Schadt, E. E.|display-authors=etal|title=An integrative genomics approach to infer causal associations between gene expression and disease|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=37|issue=7|pages=710–717|doi=10.1038/ng1589|pmid=15965475|pmc=2841396|date=2005}}</ref> that was selected by Science as one of the top 10 breakthroughs of the year in 2005.<ref>{{cite journal|author=+ See all authors and affiliations |url=https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.310.5756.1880a |title=The Runners-Up &#124; Science |journal=Science |date=2005-12-23 |volume=310 |issue=5756 |pages=1880–1885 |doi=10.1126/science.310.5756.1880a |pmid=16373539 |s2cid=32119689 |access-date=2017-06-17|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* The first publication linking a full-genome scan of [[methylation]] to a genome sequence for the [[Escherichia coli|E. coli]] microbe.<ref name="nature2"/>
* One of the earliest publications using [[microarray]]s to annotate the [[human genome]].<ref name="autogenerated2001"/>
* An editorial in Molecular Systems Biology on privacy concerns in the genome era calling for improved education of legislators, expanded non-discrimination laws, and protection of patients' rights.<ref name="nature1"/>
* A publication in Nature Genetics predicting a shift from [[Genome-wide association study|genome-wide association studies]] to integrative, network-based association studies (INAS) that take into account more types of biological data in order to discern the cause of variation in traits and diseases.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Califano A|author2=Butte AJ|author3=Friend S|author4=Ideker T|author5=Schadt EE|date=2012|title=Integrative Network-based Association Studies: Leveraging cell regulatory models in the post-GWAS era|journal=Nature Genetics|volume=44 |issue=8|pages=841–847|doi=10.1038/ng.2355|pmid=22836096|pmc=3593099}}</ref>
* A 2017 Nature Genetics paper reporting the use of functional genomics predictive network models to identify regulators of [[Inflammatory bowel disease|inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=A functional genomics predictive network model identifies regulators of inflammatory bowel disease |year=2017|pmid=28892060|last1=Peters|first1=L.
